program_meta.program_name: PhD in Computer and Information Science (CIS), Department of Computer and Information Science, School of Engineering and Applied Science (SEAS/Penn Engineering)
program_meta.sop_limit: VERBATIM (Penn Engineering Graduate Admissions 'How to Apply' page, applies to ALL Penn Engineering grad programs including CIS PhD): 'A Personal Statement. In two pages or less, write an essay that answers the questions below.' Required prompts, VERBATIM: 'Why are you interested in this program? What have you done that makes you a great candidate? How will you benefit from the program? How do you plan to contribute to the student community in Penn Engineering while you're here? Why will you succeed in the program? What will you do/accomplish once you have completed the program?' FAQ confirms, VERBATIM: 'Are there guidelines or requirements for the personal statement? No, but we do have some recommendations. For more, see How to Apply.' So the two-page ceiling + six questions IS the operative guidance; there is no separate hard word cap.
program_meta.extra_essays: NONE beyond the single Personal Statement described above (no separate diversity/personal-history statement observed on the Penn Engineering or CIS admissions pages, unlike Stanford/Purdue). Professional Resume/CV is required as a distinct upload alongside it.
program_meta.deadline_fall_2027: PhD application opens September 15, 2026; PhD application deadline December 15, 2026, 11:59 p.m. EST, per the Penn Engineering Graduate Admissions 'How to Apply' page Ph.D. Admissions Timeline, VERBATIM: '15 Sep Application opens for Fall 2027 / 15 Dec Application deadline 11:59 p.m. EST'. (Master's programs have a separate timeline: Nov 1, 2026 early deadline for CIS/Data Science/Robotics/Systems Engineering/EE/MAS-CS master's, Feb 1, 2027 regular deadline, rolling review through April 1.)
program_meta.lor_count: THREE for CIS PhD specifically (higher than the Penn Engineering default of two). program_meta.gre: OPTIONAL, university-wide, current cycle. VERBATIM (FAQ): 'Do I need to take the GRE? No – the GRE is optional for all of our graduate programs. But you're welcome to submit your scores if you've taken the GRE within the past five years.' Also VERBATIM: 'What are the minimum GRE scores you will accept? We evaluate applications as a whole portfolio, not on a single criterion, and we don't require a minimum GRE score (or a GRE score at all).' GRE institution code 2888 if submitting. Scores must be <=5 years old.
program_meta.english_test: REQUIRED FOR AKSHAT (India-born, MAHE undergraduate) UNLESS a specific waiver condition is met -- NOT a blanket India country exemption. VERBATIM waiver criteria (How to Apply, 'Test Waivers'): 'To have the English-language requirement waived, you must meet one of the following criteria by the time of matriculation: Graduate from a program in the United States; Attend school in a country in which English is recognized as the official language; or, Graduate from an institution where the medium of instruction is English, and this is indicated on the unofficial transcript.' India is NOT listed among 'countries in which English is recognized as the official language' in Penn's usual framing (that list is things like UK/Australia/Canada/Nigeria/Philippines/Singapore-type lists elsewhere at Penn) -- so Akshat's path to a waiver is the THIRD criterion: get MAHE/Manipal to indicate 'medium of instruction is English' on the unofficial transcript. If that notation is not present, TOEFL iBT/IELTS/DET is required. Accepted tests: TOEFL iBT (Penn Engineering institution code 2888; at-home administrations accepted), IELTS Academic (send electronically to 'University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science'), or Duolingo English Test (send to 'University of Pennsylvania – School of Engineering and Applied Science – Graduate'). Scores valid 2 years, must be valid at submission. RECOMMENDED (not minimum-required) scores, VERBATIM: 'TOEFL: 5.0 (or 100 on the legacy 0-120 scale); IELTS: 7.5; DET: 135.' Waiver, once qualified, 'may take 3-5 business days to reflect in your checklist' after submission.
program_meta.app_fee: $95 nonrefundable, university-wide (not CIS-specific). VERBATIM: 'Please pay the $95 nonrefundable application fee along with your online application.' No general international-applicant waiver: VERBATIM (FAQ), 'Can my application fee be waived? We do not offer fee waivers... However, you may qualify for a fee waiver if you fall into one of the following categories: U.S. citizen or permanent resident with a proven low-income background; Applicant with a Penn or U.S. military affiliation; Eligible student from a U.S. partner institution applying to an Accelerated Master's program. We do not waive the application fee for event attendance.' None of these apply to Akshat as an international applicant from India on a standard PhD track.

program_meta.advisor_model: Applicants indicate faculty interest by NAMING a potential advisor directly in the application (confirmed verbatim by faculty instructions, e.g. Eric Wong's site: 'PhD applicants: If you're interested, you will need to: 1. Apply to the CIS department. 2. Select me as a potential advisor in your application.'). This is consistent with Penn Engineering's general FAQ guidance, VERBATIM: 'Should I contact faculty members prior to applying for support for my application? Generally speaking, you don't need to contact Penn faculty prior to applying for your program; however, doctoral applicants may choose to do so to identify a principal investigator for research. Otherwise, if you have questions about the program, courses, or research, you are welcome to reach out to your department of interest.' And: 'May I contact faculty, students or alumni from the program(s) that I'm interested in? Yes, we encourage prospective students to contact the specific department you are interested in for more information.' NET READING: pre-application faculty contact is explicitly PERMITTED (not discouraged, unlike UT Austin/Berkeley), framed as optional-but-useful for identifying a PI; it is NOT required, and admission is not purely rotational -- students are admitted with a named advisor field on the application, and CIS's own PhD Advising page directs new admits to a specific Graduate Chair (Anindya De, as of this review) and Doctoral Program Manager (Britton Carnevali) rather than a lab-rotation coordinator. Cross-departmental co-advising (e.g. CIS + ESE, CIS + Radiology, CIS + Bioengineering) is common and explicitly documented (see Pratik Chaudhari's group roster, and the CIS PhD alumni list showing a student co-advised by Konrad Kording (Bioengineering) and Lyle Ungar (CIS)).
program_meta.ms_research_access: SPLIT ACROSS SIX DISTINCT MASTER'S PROGRAMS -- Akshat must pick the right one. The MSE in Computer and Information Science is the RESEARCH-CAPABLE master's: CIS's own copy states, VERBATIM, 'The Master of Science in Engineering (MSE) in Computer and Information Science degree program is designed to allow flexible planning of advanced study... Graduate studies in the Department offer the possibility for rewarding exploration and research.' By contrast, the former MCIT (Master of Computer and Information Technology) is CLOSED and being replaced by MAS-CS (Master of Applied Science in Computer Science): 'The MCIT Program is no longer accepting applications... transitioning to a new name: the Master of Applied Science in Computer Science (MAS-CS)... designed for applicants with limited or no past experience in Computer Science' -- i.e. explicitly a career-conversion, professional/terminal degree, NOT a research degree, and CIS's own page tells applicants with a CS background to apply to MSE instead: 'Candidates with an undergraduate major in Computer Science or closely related fields, should consider applying to the Master of Science in Engineering (MSE) program instead.' Since Akshat has a CS undergraduate degree, MSE-CIS (not MAS-CS) is his correct masters-track fallback if he does not go straight to PhD, and it does carry real research/thesis access.
program_meta.notes: CIS reports ~56 tenure-track/research faculty, ~995 masters students, 216 PhD students department-wide (per cis.upenn.edu/academics 2026 statistics). Applying to MULTIPLE Penn programs requires a SEPARATE application and a SEPARATE $95 fee for each (FAQ: 'You will need to upload all the required application components and pay a separate application fee for each application you submit... If you are admitted to more than one program, you may enroll in only one.'). International applicants: unofficial transcripts accepted for review; official transcripts only required upon enrollment. GRE institution code and TOEFL institution code are BOTH 2888. Key contacts named on the CIS PhD Advising page (as of this review): Britton Carnevali (CIS Doctoral Program Manager, brittonc@seas.upenn.edu / advising bookings at cisphdadvising.youcanbook.me) and Anindya De (CIS Graduate Chair, anindyad@seas.upenn.edu). faculty.research_areas: Theoretical problems in deep learning (information geometry, energy-landscape/loss-surface analysis, PAC-Bayes-style capacity control, task/transfer learning theory) and visual perception in robotics. Explicitly co-advises PhD students on medical-imaging applications with Christos Davatzikos in Radiology (fair/generalizable ML for neuroimaging) and with James Gee (deformable image matching).
faculty.why_match: Akshat's DDPM-pretraining result found a frozen diffusion encoder retains >80% of fine-tuned liver Dice but drops BELOW random initialization on kidney -- an unexplained, structure-dependent transfer failure he has not resolved. Chaudhari's research statement is built around exactly this question: what property of the data/task induces (or fails to induce) useful capacity control and transfer in a learned representation ('Does the data induce capacity control in deep learning?' is listed as a research highlight on his own site). His group's thesis 'Fair and Generalizable Machine Learning Models for Neuroimaging' (Rongguang Wang, 2024, co-advised with Christos Davatzikos in Radiology) is the closest verified Penn precedent for exactly Akshat's domain (medical imaging generalization failure across sub-populations/structures) and co-advising model (CIS/ESE + Radiology).

faculty.lab: Brachio Lab, https://brachiolab.github.io/; also part of the ASSET Center
faculty.research_areas: Debugging machine learning and making models 'do what we want them to do': robustness/adversarial ML, feature-attribution stability guarantees, interpretability/explainability with formal certification, neurosymbolic learning, LLM jailbreak/safety benchmarks, data-efficient learning with neural programs.
faculty.why_match: HiME's central claim is a CONSTRUCTIVE guarantee -- chain-rule decoding of per-level conditional sigmoids makes the predicted label set upward-closed BY CONSTRUCTION, not by post-hoc repair, at ~0.01% parameter overhead. Wong's whole research programme is about turning informal desiderata (stability, faithfulness, rule-following) into certified, provable properties of a model rather than empirical after-the-fact checks: 'Stability Guarantees for Feature Attributions with Multiplicative Smoothing' (NeurIPS 2023) and 'Probabilistic Stability Guarantees for Feature Attributions' (NeurIPS 2025) certify robustness of explanations the same way HiME certifies consistency of a hierarchical prediction. His 'Logicbreaks: A Framework for Understanding Subversion of Rule-based Inference' (ICLR 2025) is directly about when a rule-following architecture (the same idea as HiME's chain-rule decoder) can be subverted -- exactly the failure mode HiME's own limitations note (top-down error propagation from a confident shallow mistake) already flags.
faculty.key_paper_1: Probabilistic Stability Guarantees for Feature Attributions. NeurIPS, 2025.
faculty.key_paper_2: Logicbreaks: A Framework for Understanding Subversion of Rule-based Inference. ICLR, 2025. (See also: Data-Efficient Learning with Neural Programs, NeurIPS 2024; Stability Guarantees for Feature Attributions with Multiplicative Smoothing, NeurIPS 2023.)
faculty.taking_students: Yes, actively recruiting PhD students and explicit about the mechanism. Verified 2026-08-28 via his own homepage, which is current to at least NeurIPS/EMNLP 2025 presentations.
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM: 'PhD applicants: If you're interested, you will need to: 1. Apply to the CIS department. 2. Select me as a potential advisor in your application.' Separately, for masters/undergrads at Penn only: 'fill out this form. We will be in touch if there is a good fit... If you are not at UPenn, I do not currently have opportunities for external students' -- this restriction is scoped explicitly to masters/undergrad research opportunities, not PhD applicants.
faculty.email_angle: HiME makes hierarchy consistency a guarantee of the decoding rule rather than something checked after the fact; I'd like to understand where that kind of construction breaks the way your Logicbreaks work shows rule-following architectures can be subverted.
faculty.notes: Clean, unambiguous open door with a stated mechanism (select him in the application) that matches Penn CIS's stated advisor model exactly. Domain caveat: he does essentially no medical imaging -- his interpretability/robustness work is on vision/LLM benchmarks and program synthesis, not clinical data, so the fit is METHODOLOGICAL (guarantees by construction) rather than domain-matched.

faculty.why_match: Akshat's semi-supervised spine-MRI work found that per-class pseudo-label confidence thresholds calibrated on just 5 reference images match thresholds derived from 304 -- an empirical statement that a data-selection rule can be learned/calibrated far more cheaply than the full dataset would suggest. Goel's PhD thesis 'Towards Provably Efficient Algorithms for Learning Neural Networks' and her current programme on provable guarantees for learning under limited/adversarial signal are the theoretical machinery that could formalize exactly when such cheap calibration is guaranteed to generalize, rather than being an empirical coincidence of his particular dataset.

His adversarial-training tradeoff papers ('Curse of Overparameterization in Adversarial Training', 'Precise Tradeoffs for Adversarial Training') are also relevant to the robustness side of Akshat's data-centric ablations.

faculty.research_areas: Trustworthy machine learning: program synthesis and neurosymbolic methods, interpretable/verifiable ML, uncertainty quantification and conformal prediction, safe reinforcement learning. Member of ASSET, Schlein (cybersecurity), PRECISE, and PRiML centers, and PLClub.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's semi-supervised spine-MRI pipeline compared MC-dropout uncertainty against confidence thresholding for filtering pseudo-labels and found the two give comparable, largely redundant signal. Bastani's group works on conformal prediction and uncertainty quantification with formal coverage guarantees, which would let Akshat replace his ad hoc, empirically-tuned confidence/MC-dropout filter with a calibrated, provably-valid selection rule -- directly extending the open question his own ablation left unresolved (why do two different uncertainty estimators converge on the same answer, and is there a principled reason they should?).
